This glut includes both lower-purity Class 2 nickel from Indonesia and higher-purity Class 1 from China. [3] The oversupply coincided with weakened demand, notably from China's stainless steel industry, which was affected by a sluggish recovery in the country's construction sector post-COVID lockdowns. [4, 5] This imbalance has exerted significant downward pressure on nickel prices, a trend expected to continue as the global surplus persists. [3, 4] <2> In response to new US and UK sanctions on Russian metals announced on April 12, 2024, nickel prices experienced a significant upward trend. The sanctions targeted Russia's export revenues by prohibiting the import of Russian-origin aluminum, copper, and nickel into the United States and limiting their trade on global exchanges like the London Metal Exchange (LME) and Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME). This action followed an existing UK ban on Russian metal imports from December 2023. Subsequently, on April 19, 2024, the LME nickel futures price surpassed the $19,000 per ton mark, closing at $19,326 per ton. <3> On April 12, 2024, the U.S. and U.K. governments jointly announced new sanctions targeting Russian-origin nickel, aluminum, and copper to curtail Russia's revenue from metal exports. This action prohibited the import of these metals into the U.S. and barred major global exchanges, such as the London Metal Exchange (LME) and Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), from accepting new Russian-produced supplies. In immediate reaction to the news, nickel futures prices experienced a significant rally on the next trading day, Monday, April 15, 2024. The LME three-month nickel price surged, climbing to a seven-month high of $19,355 per metric ton. <4> Based on a retrospective analysis of 2023, stainless steel production in the United States declined by 9.6% year-over-year, amounting to 1.82 million tons. [2, 5] This downturn in the U.S. occurred while global stainless steel production grew by 4.6% to 58.4 million tons, driven largely by a 12.6% increase in China. [2, 5] The reduction in U.S. production, a key sector for nickel consumption, was a contributing factor to diminished nickel demand within the American market, particularly noted in the fourth quarter of 2023 when output fell by 14.2% compared to the previous quarter. This trend was largely driven by consumer hesitancy stemming from the high price of EVs, compounded by the broader cost-of-living crisis and persistent challenges with charging time and infrastructure availability. According to Deloitte’s 2024 Global Automotive Consumer Study, the number of US consumers intending to purchase an EV fell by approximately one-fifth over the last year. [1, 9] A major contributor to this surplus was a surge in the supply of lower-quality nickel pig iron from Indonesia, which now accounts for about half of the global supply. [2, 5] Concurrently, demand from the stainless steel sectors in the United States and Europe was weak. [1, 14] The situation was exacerbated by a record-high number of short positions held by investment funds on the LME, amidst global inflationary pressures and high interest rates. [1] The average LME nickel price for 2023 was $21,474 per tonne, a 16% decrease from the 2022 average. He specifically noted that demand from trucks and large EVs in the U.S. was a significant factor, with sales up 50% year-over-year. [1, 2, 4] The program is intended to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign entities for critical minerals and battery components, enhance national security, and support the growing demand for electric vehicles and stationary energy storage. This initiative aims to secure a domestic supply of nickel, a critical mineral for the manufacturing of batteries for electric vehicles and defense-related supply chains. This trend was largely driven by consumer hesitancy stemming from the high price of EVs, compounded by the broader cost-of-living crisis and persistent challenges with charging time and infrastructure availability. According to Deloitte’s 2024 Global Automotive Consumer Study, the number of US consumers intending to purchase an EV fell by approximately one-fifth over the last year. This downturn in EV demand has created significant challenges for the nickel industry, as nickel is a key component in EV batteries. The weakening demand, combined with an oversupply of the metal, has resulted in a two-year price slide for nickel, creating financial strain for mining companies. <10> In the fourth quarter of 2023, nickel prices experienced a significant decline, with the London Metal Exchange (LME) price falling to as low as $16,000 per tonne late in the year. [1] This downturn was attributed to a combination of factors, primarily a substantial surplus of nickel on the market. [1, 9] A major contributor to this surplus was a surge in the supply of lower-quality nickel pig iron from Indonesia, which now accounts for about half of the global supply. [2, 5] Concurrently, demand from the stainless steel sectors in the United States and Europe was weak. [1, 14] The situation was exacerbated by a record-high number of short positions held by investment funds on the LME, amidst global inflationary pressures and high interest rates. [1] The average LME nickel price for 2023 was $21,474 per tonne, a 16% decrease from the 2022 average. [1]

Prediction target period: from 2024-12-29 to 2025-01-09. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On December 11, 2024, a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers from the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party's (CCP) Critical Minerals Policy Working Group introduced a package of three new bills. The legislation, spearheaded by the working group's co-chairs, Rep. Rob Wittman (R-VA) and Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), aims to bolster the domestic supply chain for critical minerals and reduce the United States' dependence on foreign adversaries, particularly the People's Republic of China (PRC). Key provisions include enhancing the sustainable recycling and recovery of minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel from used batteries. The legislative package also proposes amending the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to control the export of recyclable battery materials, known as 'black mass', and magnet manufacturing byproducts, or 'swarf', to foreign adversaries by requiring a license. Additionally, the bills seek to strengthen the U.S. workforce in the critical minerals sector and foster international collaboration on earth sciences to improve supply chain resilience. <2> An industry report on the electric vehicle (EV) supply chain, published on December 3, 2024, identified that a slowdown in anticipated demand growth for critical materials was a key factor in declining prices. The analysis noted that since the beginning of 2023, lithium spot prices have fallen by 75%, while cobalt and nickel prices have declined by over 30%. This trend contributed to an EV battery price reduction of more than 25% for cathode materials globally. The report attributes the price pressure to demand growth not meeting overinflated market expectations—for example, realized lithium demand grew by 30% against a forecasted 40%—coupled with an inventory overhang in downstream sectors like battery cells and cathodes. <3> Following the U.S. presidential election in November 2024, the nickel market experienced significant volatility. [1] Prices initially increased from $16,007 per metric ton on November 4 to $16,587 on November 7. [1] However, this upward trend reversed, and the London Metal Exchange (LME) three-month nickel price fell to a four-year low of $15,540 per metric ton on November 15. [1] This decline was attributed to investor concerns over the potential economic policies of the incoming U.S. administration, particularly regarding trade with China, a top consumer of industrial metals. [1] A strengthening U.S. dollar, which reached a one-year high, and increased LME nickel inventories further contributed to the downward pressure on prices, reflecting a broader risk-off sentiment in the metals markets. [1] <4> On October 2, 2024, the nickel price on the London Metal Exchange (LME) surpassed the $18,000 per metric ton mark, reaching its highest level in three months. [2] The price continued to rise the following day, reaching around $18,200 per metric ton. [2] However, historical data for the fourth quarter of 2024 shows that after this early October peak, the price of nickel trended downward, with the monthly average for October at $16,794.6, November at $15,733.6, . [3, 4, 7] <5> On September 27, 2024, a Seeking Alpha report noted that nickel spot prices were roughly flat over the preceding month. [5] The report also highlighted a significant development in the battery manufacturing sector: on September 20, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy announced an award of over $3 billion to support 25 projects across 14 states. [1, 5, 6] This funding, part of the Biden-Harris Administration's "Investing in America" agenda, is intended to boost the domestic production of advanced batteries and battery materials. [1] The initiative is projected to create over 8,000 construction jobs and 4,000 operating positions, aiming to strengthen the U.S. supply chain for electric vehicles and grid storage. [1, 4] <6> A Wood Mackenzie report published on September 26, 2024, indicated that nickel prices experienced a slight increase in September. [1] This rise was attributed to two main factors: a 50-basis-point interest rate cut by the U.S. Federal Reserve on September 18, 2024, and a significant investment announcement by the U.S. Department of Energy (DoE). [4, 9, 11, 12] The DoE detailed plans for an investment of over $3 billion to be distributed across 25 battery manufacturing projects in 14 states, aimed at strengthening the domestic supply chain. [3, 6, 8] Despite these positive price influences, the report also cautioned that nickel demand was stumbling heading into the fourth quarter, coinciding with continued supply expansion from Indonesia. [1] <7> On September 10, 2024, Fastmarkets reported that nickel premiums in the delivered Midwest US market remained unchanged amid very slow market conditions. The nickel 4x4 cathode premium held steady at 45-55 cents per lb, a level it has maintained since February 20, 2024. Similarly, the nickel briquette premium was stable at 40-45 cents per lb, unchanged since February 27, 2024. Market participants confirmed the lack of activity, with one trader noting there had been no spot business for the preceding two weeks. <8> Nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) saw a significant increase between August 1 and August 27, 2024. [3] During this period, the LME nickel 3-month prices rose by over 5.1%, while cash settlement prices increased by more than 6.0%. [3] On Tuesday, August 27, 2024, the 3-month nickel price surpassed the $17,000 per tonne threshold again. [3] This upward trend was reported on August 28, 2024. [3] <9> Canada-based Lundin Mining Corporation announced its second-quarter 2024 results, reporting a significant downturn in nickel production due to an underground collapse at its Eagle mine in Michigan. The company stated that a 'fall of ground in the lower ramp restricted access to Eagle East, limiting production'. [3] Consequently, Lundin Mining revised its 2024 nickel production guidance downward from the original 10,000-13,000 metric tons to a new range of 7,000-9,000 metric tons. [3] The company's nickel output for the second quarter, ending June 30, 2024, was 1,721 metric tons. [3] <10> Nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) surged on May 20, 2024, with the futures price closing at a year-to-date high of $21,615 per metric ton. This significant increase pushed prices well over the $21,000 mark and was influenced by factors including China's housing stimulus measures and various global mining supply disruptions.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In early 2025, nickel prices in the United States stabilized, trading consistently between $15,000 and $15,800 per tonne, with most activity hovering around the $15,500 mark. This period of relative stability followed significant volatility resulting from geopolitical developments, specifically the restoration of pre-existing tariff structures between the United States and China. <2> In early 2025, a strong US dollar, bolstered by robust US labor market data, made nickel more expensive for international buyers, consequently reducing demand. This economic pressure was a significant factor in pushing nickel prices down to $15,078 per metric ton, the lowest level recorded in five years, with the last comparable low occurring in 2020. <3> On January 31, 2025, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) released its annual Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025. [1, 3] This comprehensive report is recognized as the earliest source of 2024 mineral production data for the world. [1, 3] The publication covers more than 90 individual nonfuel minerals and materials, including a chapter on nickel that provides five-year salient statistics for the United States and data on world production. [1, 3] For each commodity, the summary includes information on events, trends, and issues, as well as details on domestic industry structure, government programs, and tariffs. [3] <4> In January 2025, the Trump administration announced its intention to implement a 10% tariff on all goods imported from China, with the White House confirming on January 31, 2025, that the tariffs would be implemented the next day. [4, 5] The executive order, issued on February 1, 2025, cited a national emergency related to fentanyl trafficking as the basis for the tariffs, which officially went into effect on February 4, 2025. [3, 5, 6] This development, part of a broader escalation in the U.S.-China trade dispute, created significant uncertainty and added pressure on base metals markets, including nickel, within the United States. [7, 10] <5> According to an analysis by Shanghai Metal Market (SMM), China's national refined nickel production in January 2025 experienced a month-over-month decrease of 4.9%, while simultaneously showing a year-over-year increase of 18.7%. The primary reason cited for the monthly decline was the Chinese New Year holiday, during which some enterprises suspended their operations, leading to a lower industry operating rate of 69%. Despite the holiday-related slowdown and weak domestic demand, the overall supply of refined nickel remained at a high level. <6> A report from Investing News Network, published on January 7, 2025, provided a retrospective on nickel price movements from the latter half of 2024. The analysis noted that after peaking in May, nickel prices had fallen below the $16,000 per metric ton mark by the end of July 2024. Following a period of volatility in August and September, prices gained momentum at the conclusion of the third quarter, reaching $18,221 on October 2, 2024. <7> Nickel prices experienced a significant downward trend during the majority of the fourth quarter of 2024. The price per metric ton reached a peak of $18,221 on October 2 before falling to $15,732 by the end of the month. Following a brief recovery to $16,607 on November 7, prices continued to decline, hitting a 2024 low of $15,090 on December 19. The year concluded with the price at $15,300 on December 31. <8> A report published on December 16, 2024, accurately noted that the stainless steel market, a primary consumer of nickel, experienced soft demand and significant oversupply throughout 2024. This was largely driven by a substantial increase in nickel supply from Indonesia. Consequently, the nickel market remained in a surplus, exerting downward pressure on prices through the fourth quarter. Nickel prices on the LME fell 6.41% from the end of the third quarter to December 12 and hit a yearly low of US$15,090 per metric ton on December 19. Corroborating this market weakness, the North American Stainless (NAS) 304 surcharge reached its lowest quarterly average of the year in the fourth quarter, based on monthly data. <9> On December 11, 2024, a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers from the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party's (CCP) Critical Minerals Policy Working Group introduced a package of three new bills. The legislation, spearheaded by the working group's co-chairs, Rep. Rob Wittman (R-VA) and Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), aims to bolster the domestic supply chain for critical minerals and reduce the United States' dependence on foreign adversaries, particularly the People's Republic of China (PRC). Key provisions include enhancing the sustainable recycling and recovery of minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel from used batteries. The legislative package also proposes amending the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to control the export of recyclable battery materials, known as 'black mass', and magnet manufacturing byproducts, or 'swarf', to foreign adversaries by requiring a license. Additionally, the bills seek to strengthen the U.S. workforce in the critical minerals sector and foster international collaboration on earth sciences to improve supply chain resilience. <10> An industry report on the electric vehicle (EV) supply chain, published on December 3, 2024, identified that a slowdown in anticipated demand growth for critical materials was a key factor in declining prices. The analysis noted that since the beginning of 2023, lithium spot prices have fallen by 75%, while cobalt and nickel prices have declined by over 30%. This trend contributed to an EV battery price reduction of more than 25% for cathode materials globally. The report attributes the price pressure to demand growth not meeting overinflated market expectations—for example, realized lithium demand grew by 30% against a forecasted 40%—coupled with an inventory overhang in downstream sectors like battery cells and cathodes.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order titled "Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production" to bolster the domestic supply of critical minerals and reduce the nation's reliance on foreign sources. The order aims to facilitate and expedite all stages of mineral production, including mining, processing, refining, and smelting. Citing threats to national and economic security from dependence on hostile foreign powers, the directive calls for immediate action to increase domestic production to the fullest extent possible. The order expands the definition of "critical minerals" to include uranium, copper, potash, and gold, among others to be determined. Key provisions include fast-tracking the permitting process for mining projects, identifying federal lands for mineral extraction, and mobilizing public and private capital, partly by invoking the Defense Production Act, to support the industry. The order sets aggressive deadlines for federal agencies to identify priority projects and facilitate their approval. <2> In early 2025, nickel prices in the United States stabilized, trading consistently between $15,000 and $15,800 per tonne, with most activity hovering around the $15,500 mark. This period of relative stability followed significant volatility resulting from geopolitical developments, specifically the restoration of pre-existing tariff structures between the United States and China. <3> In early 2025, a strong US dollar, bolstered by robust US labor market data, made nickel more expensive for international buyers, consequently reducing demand. This economic pressure was a significant factor in pushing nickel prices down to $15,078 per metric ton, the lowest level recorded in five years, with the last comparable low occurring in 2020. <4> On January 31, 2025, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) released its annual Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025. [1, 3] This comprehensive report is recognized as the earliest source of 2024 mineral production data for the world. [3, 5, 6] This development, part of a broader escalation in the U.S.-China trade dispute, created significant uncertainty and added pressure on base metals markets, including nickel, within the United States. The year concluded with the price at $15,300 on December 31. <9> A report published on December 16, 2024, accurately noted that the stainless steel market, a primary consumer of nickel, experienced soft demand and significant oversupply throughout 2024. This was largely driven by a substantial increase in nickel supply from Indonesia. Consequently, the nickel market remained in a surplus, exerting downward pressure on prices through the fourth quarter. Nickel prices on the LME fell 6.41% from the end of the third quarter to December 12 and hit a yearly low of US$15,090 per metric ton on December 19. Corroborating this market weakness, the North American Stainless (NAS) 304 surcharge reached its lowest quarterly average of the year in the fourth quarter, based on monthly data. <10> On December 11, 2024, a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers from the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party's (CCP) Critical Minerals Policy Working Group introduced a package of three new bills. The legislation, spearheaded by the working group's co-chairs, Rep. Rob Wittman (R-VA) and Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), aims to bolster the domestic supply chain for critical minerals and reduce the United States' dependence on foreign adversaries, particularly the People's Republic of China (PRC). Key provisions include enhancing the sustainable recycling and recovery of minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel from used batteries. The legislative package also proposes amending the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to control the export of recyclable battery materials, known as 'black mass', and magnet manufacturing byproducts, or 'swarf', to foreign adversaries by requiring a license. Additionally, the bills seek to strengthen the U.S. workforce in the critical minerals sector and foster international collaboration on earth sciences to improve supply chain resilience.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Driven by Indonesian supply management policies and broader macroeconomic factors, global nickel prices impacting the U.S. market experienced a significant rally starting in mid-December 2025. Sparked by Indonesia's decisions to delay mining permits and cut nickel output quotas to support prices, the metal surged by approximately 30% from its mid-December levels. By early January 2026, prices surpassed $18,000 per tonne, hitting 15-month highs and marking a notable structural shift toward active supply management in the global nickel market. <2> On December 18, 2025, Talon Metals announced a definitive share purchase agreement to acquire Lundin Mining's subsidiary, which indirectly holds the Eagle Mine and the Humboldt Mill in Michigan. The acquisition creates a pure-play U.S. nickel company anchored by the Eagle Mine, currently the only operating primary nickel mine in the United States. The deal is expected to close in early January 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. <3> The U.S. government allocated $7.5 billion for critical minerals under the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act'. As part of this initiative, $2 billion was directed to the National Defense Stockpile's Transaction Fund to secure essential materials, including nickel, copper, lithium, antimony, and 16 rare earth elements. <4> Ford Motor Company announced a massive $19.5 billion write-down tied to a strategic pivot away from fully electric vehicles, redirecting capital and factory capacity toward hybrid and gasoline-powered options. This significant pullback by a major automaker eroded the U.S. battery demand pillar for nickel, contributing to softer domestic nickel prices in late 2025. <5> On November 14, 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced two funding opportunities totaling over $355 million to strengthen domestic critical minerals supply chains. This funding is part of a broader $1 billion critical minerals initiative announced in August 2025. Applications for the two programs, which aim to expand the domestic production of materials essential for energy, manufacturing, transportation, and national defense, are due by December 15, 2025. <6> On November 12, 2025, the United States Mint struck its final circulating penny, concluding 232 years of production due to rising material costs. With the penny's elimination, the five-cent nickel became the lowest-value U.S. coin in production. This milestone has sparked intense debate over the nickel's viability, as elevated base metal prices have driven its production cost up to nearly 14 cents per coin. <7> A market analysis published on November 12, 2025, highlighted the anticipated economic impact of new legislation ending the U.S. $7,500 electric vehicle (EV) tax credit. Initially, under the Inflation Reduction Act, this credit was set to expire in 2032. However, a new law signed on July 4, 2025, accelerated the expiration date to September 30, 2025. This policy change is expected to reduce the affordability of EVs, particularly for middle-class consumers, and consequently slow adoption rates. The accelerated expiration is also predicted to weaken the near-term demand for Class 1 nickel, a critical component in high-energy-density batteries, adding significant pressure to the demand side of the nickel market. <8> Major U.S. automaker Stellantis has provided notice to terminate its binding offtake agreement with Australia's Alliance Nickel for battery-grade nickel and cobalt from the NiWest project in Western Australia. The termination, which takes effect on December 3, 2025, was driven by challenging nickel market conditions, weak global prices, and related project financing constraints that stalled progress on the mine's development. <9> The World Steel Association announced that U.S. crude steel production reached 6.9 million tonnes in September 2025, marking a 6.7% increase compared to the same month in 2024. This year-over-year growth in a key end-use market for primary nickel is seen as a positive economic indicator amidst discussions of weaker demand. The report, which covers 70 countries, noted that total world crude steel production was 141.8 million tonnes in September 2025. <10> A report on North American nickel prices for the third quarter of 2025 revealed that in September, prices averaged $15.26 USD/KG, a 2.8% decline. This decrease was attributed to reduced demand from the automotive and stainless steel sectors. The decline in the automotive sector was specifically linked to the end of the U.S. EV tax credit on September 30, which increased new vehicle costs for consumers. Despite the softer pricing, the regional market was assessed as being relatively balanced.
